messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Harold is a 69-year-old widowed financial analyst who was referred for psychological assessment following a prolonged period of functional decline and emotional dysregulation in the months after his wife's death. His PCL-5 score of 74 places him in the severe range, and the clinical picture that has emerged across the intake and early sessions is one of a man caught in a tightening loop of intrusion, physiological alarm, and desperate suppression that has, by his own reckoning, made the last year of his life nearly unlivable.

The traumatic event itself was not sudden. Harold watched his wife, Diane, deteriorate over fourteen months from a diagnosis of aggressive pancreatic cancer to her death in the hospital room where he sat holding her hand. What he has described most haltingly is not the death itself but a specific afternoon three weeks before the end, when Diane, heavily medicated and barely conscious, suddenly gripped his wrist and said his name with a clarity she had not shown in days. He understood in that moment, with a certainty he has never been able to shake, that she was frightened, and that there was nothing he could do. He left the hospital that evening and drove home alone through streets that looked, he said, like they belonged to someone else's life.

In the months that followed, Harold found that certain moments in his environment carried that afternoon back to him with brutal immediacy. A colleague mentioning a parent's illness during a team call, a radio segment about hospice care, the word "loss" appearing in a client's estate planning document — any of these could produce a sudden, unbidden return of the hospital room, the fluorescent light, Diane's grip on his wrist. These triggers did not merely recall the memory; they reliably produced a cascade of physical reactivity — his chest would tighten, his hands would tremble over his keyboard, his heart would accelerate in a way he described as feeling like a warning — and with that came waves of guilt, horror, and a shame he struggled to articulate, rooted in his belief that he had somehow failed her in her fear. The physical alarm and the emotional intensity of those moments felt to Harold like evidence that something was genuinely wrong with him, which itself kept his attention narrowed toward anything that might signal another intrusion, so that ordinary cues — a quiet office, a phone ringing unexpectedly — were scanned for threat and, when they arrived, amplified what was already there.

Harold's response to this was to construct, methodically and with the discipline of a man who had spent four decades managing risk, a life organized around avoidance. He declined invitations to a colleague's retirement gathering because he knew there would be toasts, and toasts meant reflection on time passing and people gone. He stopped attending his church, where grief and mortality were subjects that arose without warning. He routed his morning commute away from the cemetery where Diane was buried. At work, he began deflecting any conversation that touched on loss themes with a brisk efficiency his younger colleagues have apparently taken for coldness. The numbing he employed was deliberate — he described it as "turning a dial down" — and the suppression of intrusive thoughts was effortful and constant. What Harold had not anticipated was that this architecture of avoidance, rather than protecting him, seemed to make the triggers more potent when they did break through; the suppressed material returned with greater force, and the physical reactivity that followed was, if anything, worse for the silence around it. His irritability, which he had initially attributed to grief, had become a source of rupture at work — a sharp exchange with a junior analyst over a minor error had been escalated to HR, and it was this incident, more than anything, that finally brought him to seek help.

Harold arrives at sessions punctual and formally dressed, a man who has held himself together through structure. What he is most afraid of, he said in their second meeting, is that the feelings will never become manageable. What he hopes for, more quietly, is to be able to visit Diane's grave without his body turning against him.
